title: A spatio-temporal method for crime prediction using historical crime data and transitional zones identified from nightlight imagery
thesis: Proposes a spatio-temporal Cokriging algorithm integrating historical crime data and urban transitional zones (from nightlight imagery) to improve crime prediction accuracy in Cincinnati.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. The paper does not discuss dual-use, technology transfer, or the economic properties of data as information goods. It focuses on crime prediction methodology.
theme_2_justification: Not addressed. The paper does not discuss algorithmic opacity, epistemic authority of data, surveillance as knowledge production, or democratic deficits. It is a technical prediction study.
theme_3_justification: Tangential mention. The paper treats the city as a programmable system for crime prediction (e.g., 'crime generators and attractors' along transitional zones, use of kernel density for continuous risk maps), but does not engage with modulation, ambient control, or smart city governance as a mode of social sorting.
theme_4_justification: Not addressed. No discussion of spatial destruction, weaponisation of infrastructure, home unmaking, or urban warfare.
notes: Standard quantitative GIScience paper on crime prediction. No engagement with dual-use, surveillance, or socio-political dimensions of algorithmic governance.
